title: Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network
description: US President Donald Trump has denied limiting Ukraine's access to Starlink's sister internet network Starshield after it restricted drone speed, hampe
body: US President Donald Trump has denied limiting Ukraine's access to Starlink's sister internet network Starshield after it restricted drone speed, hampering Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks."It wasn't me and I don't think it was [Starlink owner] Elon [Musk]," Trump said, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said speed had yet to be restored.Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions, while Reuters news agency reported on Thursday that the order had come from inside the White House.Ukraine was hit by several deadly strikes on Tuesday after the network slowdown.Starlink is a civilian-use high-speed internet network operated by Musk's SpaceX. Starshield - which relies on Starlink- is its military-grade sister service that was designed for the Pentagon.The US had previously warned it could withhold sharing intelligence, crucial for Kyiv's defences, if Ukraine did not stop hitting Russian oil refineries.Tension has been brewing between Washington and Kyiv for days over a recent controversial diesel deal between Russia and the US.Zelensky - angered by the deal - resumed targeting Russian oil refineries this week in a move criticised by Trump three days after he announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Kyiv said it would stop the strikes if Russia did the same but Moscow  never confirmed the ceasefire and continued its attacks. "If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" Zelensky asked EU leaders at a summit on Friday.Trump had also said that Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin".But speaking to reporters as he left the White House on Friday, the US president said he had a good relationship with his Ukrainian counterpart.Asked about Starshield, he said he was "not sure" it "ever came down".Musk earlier explained that Starshield was managed by the US government, and that the Pentagon could have been responsible.In its report about the alleged order regarding Starshield, Reuters quoted two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.On Tuesday night, Starlink restricted speed limits to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.Some 600,000 in Ukraine were left without power as communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military were also hit in the deadly attacks.A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an investigation into the disruptions to the network."Restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure," the letter read.On Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron vowed that EU states would not abandon Ukraine.  Speaking at the end of the two-day summit in Brussels attended by Zelensky, Macron said it was Europe's job to hold the line in the face of some people's "ambiguities". That was apparently a reference to signs of wavering US support for Ukraine. Funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another freezing winter - its fifth since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - topped the summit's agenda.The war will cost €155bn (£131bn; $174bn) next year, Zelensky told the European Council, with at least €70bn needed to come from the EU for defence and weapons.Macron said Europe was working to help Ukraine with its satellite and early warning systems, and Ukraine's friends would look at its request for further aid.

schema.headline: Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network

title: White House defends new press secretary Katie Zacharia over her legal credentials
description: The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.President Donald Trump describe
body: The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week. She has referred to herself as a lawyer. But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China." She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people".Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association.It is seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime".The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed.A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US. The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself. She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney.The new press secretary also told the paper that when she answered China to a question about her bar exam, it was a misunderstanding. She had mistakenly thought, above the din of Marine One, the reporter had asked: "Where were you after law school?"Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass.A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be.She moved to Beijing because of her husband's job at an American private equity firm. Zacharia has said she worked on "international transaction law" there.Her LinkedIn profile states that she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13.In China, only Chinese citizens are eligible to obtain a licence to practise law. Foreign employees may work at law firms in other roles.In February last year, Zacharia said on conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show that she had worked as outside counsel for the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the World Bank during her time in China.The BBC has contacted the World Bank and IFC for comment, as well as Zhong Lun Law Firm.It is understood the World Bank Group sometimes retains outside law firms, and that those firms decide which of their lawyers are assigned to which parts of any work. Zacharia has also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally Ric Grenell, according to her LinkedIn profile.

schema.headline: White House defends new press secretary Katie Zacharia over her legal credentials

title: Maduro pleads not guilty to additional charges in New York
description: Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared in court on Thursday to plead not guilty to new charges of conspiracy to
body: Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared in court on Thursday to plead not guilty to new charges of conspiracy to commit torture.The US government initially accused Maduro of narco-terrorism, drug trafficking and weapons-related offenses, before adding new charges against him and Flores last week.Maduro and Flores were captured in January during a US military raid, after which they were taken to New York, where they remain in jail.The couple has pleaded not guilty to the allegations and both have argued to have the case thrown out on the grounds that they qualify for sovereign immunity. Their trial is scheduled for June 2027.In a new indictment last week, government prosecutors alleged Maduro and Flores "created and maintained a violent system of repression" that saw "thousands of Venezuelans" killed, harassed, and tortured.Nicolas Maduro denied the new charges brought against him by the US government, telling a court on Thursday he denied the "false accusations and false testimony against me.""I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in Spanish through a translator.Judge Alvin Hellerstein interrupted Maduro, and declared the court would enter a plea of not guilty for Maduro."I am completely innocent. I am not guilty," Flores said through a translator.Maduro and Flores wore beige jail uniforms and both appear to have lost weight during their detention in Brooklyn.The alleged torture methods included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture", the indictment states.The US also accused Maduro of authorising the use of torture "against specific individuals" and alleges US citizens were tortured under this system.Prosecutors already have accused Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices of engaging in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnering with cartels designated as terrorist groups.Maduro previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.He and his wife's lawyers have argued that Maduro is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal.Flores unsuccessfully petitioned a judge to allow her to be released on bond while she awaited trial, arguing she had heart problems and other health issues while detained at the notorious Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.

schema.headline: Maduro pleads not guilty to additional charges in New York

title: Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
description: Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a diffe
body: Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of Durrës, Shkodër, Lezhë and Vlora in the west, Gjirokastër in the south and Korçë in the east.The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living.Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers.Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons.Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony.Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation. A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too. The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president.They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night. But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands.The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership.Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement.Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard."Another called Brunela told the BBC's What in the World programme she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth."An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward.After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system. Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos."All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday.The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward".Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama.But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance.So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it.On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved. Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU.Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday."These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence."

schema.headline: Albanian protests turn violent: What we know

title: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills five, minister says
description: Five people have been killed and 16 injured in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, w
body: Five people have been killed and 16 injured in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say.Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace.The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden".A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis.Yemeni health minister Qasim Buhaibeh said the casualties included "those working to guard the site and civilian employees".The country's Prime Minister Shaya Zindani condemned the Houthis' attack on Aden, calling it "cowardly" and a "continuation of their criminal behaviour".He said the government continued to carry out its duties and vowed that it would not weaken the resolve of its forces to continue operations against the Houthis on Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and other front lines.Earlier, the Houthis denied that they had attacked Saudi Arabia on Thursday, after the coalition said its forces had intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest shrines.The Houthis have been launching missiles and drones at airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the strikes on the territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.On Saturday, a Houthi missile strike killed 13 people at Riyadh's international airport, which was the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis to escalate their conflict with the kingdom."Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions," Rayed Krimly told reporters, according to AFP news agency."We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.There was no immediate response from Iran's government. However, it has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and said it only supports them politically.Iran's foreign minister has also said it is ready to provide "any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks" between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.At least 1,282 people have been killed and 5,890 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.The UN says another 201,000 people have been displaced and that there has been an alarming surge in suspected cholera cases.

schema.headline: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills five, minister says

title: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
description: Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the
body: Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume.Zelensky said he had restricted attacks for three days while Russia continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times, external.Russian President Vladimir Putin said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine denied - but there had been no "significant damage".Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks but Ukrainian defence sources later told the BBC some functionality on Starlink satellite services had resumed.They said "operation while on the move", part of Starlink's military service Starshield, had been restored, although it remains unclear whether restrictions on the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection have been fully lifted.Officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances" behind the move, the sources added.In a separate development, seven people are missing after a drone attack set a chemical tanker on fire off Romania, according to naval officials. Moscow said it had hit two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port, without naming them.The Kremlin said Kyiv had "attempted a large-scale attack" on a refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris caused a fire at the site in Ryazan. Zelensky said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.He previously said he would agree to the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal.Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.European leaders have rallied around the Ukrainian president. Italy's Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC that the US restricting its intelligence-sharing with Kyiv would be a "complete mistake"."Because it is a fundamental form of support. This means denying a country any chance of defending itself."He added: "Peace will be achieved when Putin will be convinced that there is a stalemate... that he cannot advance anymore. But if he sees a weakness on the Ukrainian front, if the United States takes its resources away, then Putin will think he can win, and so he will continue the war."Zelensky met Nato chief Mark Rutte as a two-day summit of European leaders began in Brussels on Thursday. The head of the military alliance said they had discussed "the importance of implementing an energy ceasefire as well as Nato allies' continuous support for Ukraine".Zelensky told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.There were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame for the sudden Starlink restrictions on Tuesday evening, but owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this and suggested it was the Trump administration's doing. "It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing. Starlink's sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US defence department contract. The BBC has approached the US authorities for comment.That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which has sent fuel costs skyrocketing.Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence.Local officials report at least 13 people were killed across Ukraine on Wednesday in what Zelensky called a "constant", large-scale Russian attack. He said more than 850 drones had been launched at dozens of cities and communities.At least three people were killed in the central region of Kirovohrad as it suffered its largest attack since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022, officials there said, with nearly 360 drones launched during a 10-hour barrage. Deaths were also reported in Donetsk, Kherson and Volyn."It is clear that Russia deliberately escalated these attacks, taking advantage of the easing of sanctions and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelensky wrote on social media.

schema.headline: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume

title: Peshawar: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after Pakistan school roof collapses
description: At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital
body: At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials.More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition.Emergency services were called to the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, rescue official Bilal Faizi told the BBC.The roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, he said, causing ceilings below to cave in and trap children beneath the debris.Announcing the arrest of the school's owner, police chief Mian Saeed promised a thorough inquiry into "whether there were any violations of building codes".Warning: This article contains distressing detailsAn English teacher from a nearby school said he immediately rushed to the site with other local residents when they heard sirens and the sound of ambulances.Together, they pulled more than 20 children from the rubble, he said."I personally pulled out six children with my own hands. Most of them were alive and talking. But later it was found that they had passed away.""There was a lot of blood," he said. "One child said he was in a lot of pain. His tongue had dried up in his mouth, [and he was] asking for water."Sohail, another local resident, said he and others tried to remove children from under the rubble "using shovels".The school building had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak. Earlier reports suggested the destroyed classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down.There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said.It appears that when the roof of the top-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too.Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear.The school is on a very narrow street, meaning it was difficult for rescue workers to reach the site and transport the injured to hospitals.Peshawar's Lady Reading Hospital reported the deaths of 32 children and a teacher while Naseerullah Khan Babar Memorial Hospital reported one child dead.

schema.headline: Peshawar: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after Pakistan school roof collapses

title: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontlineByDan JohnsonUkraine correspondent Reporting fromnear L
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontlineByDan JohnsonUkraine correspondent Reporting fromnear Lyman, eastern UkraineA Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months. The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September –  and suffered few casualties in return.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The Starlink system was integrated into Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, but this week Kyiv said restrictions had been imposed on it without warningThe Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.Image caption, Ukraine's military says it has liberated 277 sq km in the eastern Donbas regionHe is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability. Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBCImage caption, Dealer, a soldier in the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, just came off the front lineAn infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous"."The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBCImage caption, Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unitIn Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation."As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed.""I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present."The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained."This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBCImage caption, Nets now span roads in eastern Ukraine to protect from dronesAll this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin. Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."Additional reporting by Kostas Kallergis and Anastasiia Levchenko

schema.headline: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role

title: Barack Obama tells Glasgow audience drift towards extremism 'not inevitable'
description: Obama said that during his presidential campaign in 2008, when social media and technology was gaining traction, he had seen them as a beacon for hope
body: Obama said that during his presidential campaign in 2008, when social media and technology was gaining traction, he had seen them as a beacon for hopeBut he said the same positive forces and tools that could mobilise people around democracy or human rights could also be used by hate groups.He said they "connected people for good, but also for ill"."It turns out that the reptilian side of our brain really gets attracted to anger, fear, resentment and the sense that someone is out to get you," he said."So a lot of social media and a lot of our information is informed around that."But the former president, who has already spoken in Belfast and will appear in Manchester on Thursday night, said that a drift towards extremism was "not inevitable".He added: "After World War Two, at least in the United States and certainly in Europe as well, the federal government said 'we're going to set up some rules because we've seen what propaganda can do in the hands of somebody like Hitler. "We can see how big lies and misinformation can distort and enrage and incite violence. So we're going to hold these folks responsible'.""We have not chosen to do that."Speaking about hope, Obama was asked if he still believed in a Martin Luther King Jr phrase he quoted years ago, about the arm of the moral universe being long, but ultimately bending towards justice.The former president said that he still stands by the quote and argued that hope is an active "almost theological" choice people must make.He said: "It is a decision about how do we face and embrace this finite amount of time we have on the planet." He told the audience he believes it is healthier for people to believe that change is possible."I think when we act on that basis, it doesn't always work out, but over time things do get better," he said.Obama also said there seems to be a cycle in humanity where people forget lessons learned from the past and start to take things for granted."We start thinking 'maybe using language in public from our politicians that fosters hatred and scapegoats certain people – immigrants, Jews, or blacks or gays – that's just talk, it's humour'."He said people forget where that can lead to, with them becoming less tolerant.Obama told the audience that the world is going to be dealing with "big challenges", but he said he thinks "we can be better" and that making the world better remains worth fighting for.

schema.headline: Barack Obama tells Glasgow audience drift towards extremism 'not inevitable'

title: Three things we learned from the US midterm debates
description: Republicans running for office are facing the same question they have been asked in elections since 2016: how aligned are they with President Donald T
body: Republicans running for office are facing the same question they have been asked in elections since 2016: how aligned are they with President Donald Trump?Conservatives who have bucked the president in the past have generally not fared well with voters. The president has seen low approval ratings in recent months, with polls suggesting voters are largely concerned with the cost of living and high fuel prices.While some Republican candidates have remained in lockstep with Trump, a Reuters analysis indicated, external that two-thirds of candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with the president in some way this election cycle.Susan Collins, a Maine Republican running for her sixth term in the Senate who has repeatedly broken with Trump, is again putting clear distance between herself and the president. "I voted with President Biden 91% of the time," Collins said during a debate last week."The fact is, this year alone, this Congress alone, I voted against President Trump 137 times," she said.Collins is fighting a tighter Senate race than she expected against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. A New York Times/Siena University poll from mid-September suggests Collins could be ahead in that race by 3%, while others indicate Jackson is in the lead.There are 35 Senate seats up for grabs this November, but in 21 there are no debates scheduled among the main candidates, an ABC News analysis found.One race's lack of debates has surprised many observers: the Texas contest between James Talarico, a Democratic state representative, and Ken Paxton, a Republican and former state attorney general.Polls in the typically Republican state suggest that Talarico could be in reach of a surprise win. Should he succeed, he could help give Democrats control of the US Senate by flipping one of the four seats they need to create a majority.Talarico has accepted four debate invitations from different news networks. Paxton, meanwhile, has not accepted any of those invitations. In July, Paxton's campaign spokesperson told media outlets that he would debate Talarico. But since then, the campaign, and Paxton, have said little on the matter. Trump, who backed Paxton in the Republican primaries, has even urged the candidates to debate."One thing about not showing up is you lose the opportunity to make the case for yourself, and instead, what you do is you give your opponent the ability and the opportunity to make your case as negative as possible," Peter Trumbore, a political science professor at Oakland University, told the BBC's US partner CBS News last month.

schema.headline: Three things we learned from the US midterm debates

title: Mpumalanga rehab centre: South African police rescue 200 people, some in chains
description: A pastor and his wife have been arrested in South Africa after 200 people, some in chains, were found held at a suspected illegal rehabilitation centr
body: A pastor and his wife have been arrested in South Africa after 200 people, some in chains, were found held at a suspected illegal rehabilitation centre in the north-eastern part of the country.The facility, operated from a church in Mpumalanga province, was discovered during an operation by officials in the area on Thursday.Authorities said they uncovered "gross inhumane conditions" when they raided the facility, with some patients found with "sores all over their bodies" and "others chained to each other".Police have since charged the couple, who were running the facility, with kidnapping but could add more charges. They have not yet commented.Illegal rehabilitation centres have mushroomed in South Africa in recent years as drug use spirals in the country.Last year, the department of social development said it had uncovered over 100 unlawful facilities operating across the country, mostly in Gauteng province, home to the country's largest city, Johannesburg.A girl of 16 and a boy of 11 were found being kept in the same room as adults in the Mpumalanga centre.The couple running it told officials they were housing 60 people, but upon inspection, more than three times that number were found, including more than 30 women.The group, mostly believed to be drug addicts, were found in crowded rooms and without access to functioning bathrooms or running water."Some [of them had] been at the alleged illegal centre for a while," the department said.Gift Skhosana, one of those held at the facility, told local broadcaster Newzroom Afrika it was "common practice" for patients to be chained."They chain us as punishment [and] when you gain entry," he said. Despite this, Skhosana, who was a drug user, said the facility helped him get clean and overcome his addiction.Another person, who was not named, said his experience with the facility left him needing help mentally.The couple charged a monthly fee of 3,000 rand ($182; £137) to house the patients, of which almost a half would go to the church.Fourteen of those found at the centre have since been taken to hospital for further medical treatment, police said.Officials said 132 have been reunited with their families. The couple is expected to appear in a local court on Monday.

schema.headline: Mpumalanga rehab centre: South African police rescue 200 people, some in chains

title: School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey
description: "You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at th
body: "You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school.The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?"Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad.Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people.Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that. President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail.Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally.But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni.The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order".Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class.According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since. The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed.Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN).Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran.The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself.On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites.A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility.Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families."A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said.The row has now spilled over into Turkey, Baku's closest ally, which provided vital support during Azerbaijan's 2020 war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh.The two countries call themselves "one nation, two states".President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a devout Muslim, has spoken of creating a "pious generation".   His chief adviser, Oktay Saral, has called the Azerbaijani restrictions "unacceptable" and urged Baku to "reverse this mistake"."A headscarf is not an obstacle; it is a requirement of one's faith!" Saral wrote on X.Several MPs from Turkey's governing AK Party joined in. Small demonstrations were held outside Azerbaijan's embassy in Ankara, organised by Köklü Değişim, an Islamist movement linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, and outside its consulate in Istanbul, organised by conservative Islamist group Özgür-Der.President Aliyev's New Azerbaijan Party accused Turkish officials of an "openly defamatory" information campaign and of "baseless accusations", warning that Oktay Saral's comments risked harming ties, and cautioned against interference in Azerbaijan's internal affairs.Earlier this month, Ilham Aliyev himself said no one should "stick their noses into our way of life".Behind the dispute there may lie another source of friction. Turkish protesters have linked the headscarf rules to Azerbaijan's close ties with Israel, which sells weapons to Baku and buys Azerbaijani oil.Turkey's relations with Israel have collapsed over Gaza, but Azerbaijan has tried to maintain relationships with both countries.That is a difficult balancing act. On Thursday, when Israel's President Isaac Herzog addressed a regional security summit hosted by Azerbaijan in Baku, delegations from Turkey, Iran and other countries walked out of the hall.

schema.headline: School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey

title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
description: ByJoshua CheethamThomas Copeland and Alison BenjaminBBC VerifyThe number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz
body: ByJoshua CheethamThomas Copeland and Alison BenjaminBBC VerifyThe number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacksThe aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".Oil shipments stallMiddle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day"."The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.Additional reporting by Becky DaleGraphics by Tom Shiel and Mark Edwards

schema.headline: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow

title: Inside Brooklyn novelty shop at centre of 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
description: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.Inside,
body: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000)."Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a  shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale. It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day."Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said. "It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises. One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy. For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise.Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days. Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here."I really like it here."

schema.headline: Inside Brooklyn novelty shop at centre of 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird

title: CJP, Abhijeet Dipke: 'Cockroach' party founder detained ahead of Central Park Delhi protest
description: Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of India's "cockroach" movement, and a few others were detained in Delhi as police tried to stop a protest demanding the r
body: Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of India's "cockroach" movement, and a few others were detained in Delhi as police tried to stop a protest demanding the resignation of the country's election chief.Hundreds had gathered in Connaught Place, one of the capital's busiest commercial districts, waving Indian flags and shouting slogans despite a heavy security presence.Police sealed off Central Park, the planned site of the protest, and deployed thousands of police and paramilitary personnel to prevent the gathering.The Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) accuses India's Election Commission of manipulating voter lists to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling BJP. Both deny the allegation.The group has held a series of protests in Delhi in recent weeks, with police repeatedly detaining its leaders and supporters. Friday's demonstration unfolded under similarly heavy security presence, though the police response was more restrained than during last weekend's sweeping crackdown.Hours before the protest, police went to the house where Dipke was staying. In an exchange broadcast live on Instagram, he challenged officers who had come to caution him against holding the march, asking whether waving the Indian flag was against the law.Hours later, the BBC saw officers surround Dipke as he approached his car and force him into a police vehicle. Some supporters tried to stop it from leaving.It was Dipke's second detention in less than a week. Last Saturday, police had boarded his plane shortly after it landed in Delhi to prevent him from reaching another demonstration. He was released the following day.The movement's two other main leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were also detained last weekend and later released. But on Wednesday, they were sent to jail for five days after returning to Jantar Mantar, a protest site near parliament that police had recently declared off-limits. Friday's march was partly intended to demand the release of Das and Ranka.Dipke's detention means the movement's three main leaders are once again in custody.The CJP said it had lost contact with him and accused police of taking him to an undisclosed location and denying him access to lawyers.But they insist the arrests and detentions will not stop them. "They may detain three people, but how will they stop 30 tomorrow? How will they stop 300 leaders?" CJP spokesperson Mehr Pasricha told the BBC.Police have not publicly confirmed the grounds for Dipke's detention or responded to the CJP's latest allegations.Anish Gawande, the opposition politician who had been hosting Dipke, also questioned the police action."Detaining a lone man walking with the national flag in his hand is a bit of a joke," he said.At Connaught Place, the police presence dwarfed the protest itself. Around 200-300 people initially gathered outside Central Park, which authorities had closed. Unable to enter, they walked around its perimeter, waving Indian flags and shouting slogans. More protesters arrived as the evening progressed.Officers kept emerging from buses parked around the district. Journalists crowded the streets too, and together with police, they far outnumbered the demonstrators.For much of the evening, police largely held back, with the BBC witnessing only a handful of detentions. But as darkness fell, officers began using force against some protesters.The BBC saw some young demonstrators being pushed into a bus where women were already being held. Inside were around 50 female officers, far more than the number of detainees.The BBC also saw two people being injured during the police action. One protester fell to the ground and appeared to have hurt their leg.Among those detained was Neha Bora, a prominent leader of the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) who has emerged as one of the faces of the recent protests. She had also been detained during last weekend's crackdown.Barely five months old, the CJP began as an online campaign in May after India's chief justice likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches. Dipke embraced the insult and turned it into a rallying cry.By July, the group had become a formidable force, drawing thousands of young people into protests over leaked exam papers. A march towards parliament in July descended into clashes with police, bringing the movement wider attention and intensifying pressure on the government. The unrest eventually forced the resignation of India's education minister.The CJP has since turned its attention to India's electoral system, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a sweeping revision of voter lists known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).Critics say the exercise risks removing legitimate voters from the rolls, potentially depriving them of the right to vote. The Election Commission says it is targeting ineligible, dead and duplicate voters and denies allegations that it is favouring the ruling BJP.Last weekend, authorities imposed severe restrictions to stop CJP supporters from reaching a planned rally, sealing off roads, shutting metro stations and deploying thousands of security personnel across Delhi.The BBC witnessed, external dozens of protesters being detained across the capital, including students and journalists.The action drew criticism but police defended it as necessary to maintain public order and prevent unauthorised gatherings.Dipke, Das and Ranka were released the following day after agreeing to maintain peace and good behaviour. But the dispute over where they could protest was only beginning.Police removed Jantar Mantar from Delhi's list of approved protest sites, naming three alternative venues.Built in the 18th Century to study the stars, the observatory stands close to Parliament and has long been one of India's most recognisable stages for public dissent. The CJP accused authorities of trying to push demonstrations away from the seat of power.On Tuesday, Das and Ranka returned to the restricted site with a handful of supporters, unfurling the Indian flag and shouting slogans against Kumar.Police said some protesters had climbed over a locked gate and that the organisers had breached the conditions of their release. The following day, the two men were sent to jail for five days.The arrests did little to deter the movement from announcing another demonstration.In a video message on Thursday, Dipke urged supporters unable to travel to Delhi to raise the Indian flag in their own towns and cities. He also acknowledged the possibility of being arrested again."I also may be jailed after this, but I am not worried. Tricolour is my pride and I will raise it," he said.By Friday morning, police had served him with a notice warning against holding the march without permission.Authorities closed Central Park for two days, citing "administrative reasons", and offered to let a small group wave the national flag and sing the anthem at another location.The CJP came up with a different plan. Supporters were told to enter Connaught Place in groups of fewer than five, unfurl the flag, take a photograph and leave."Waving the Tiranga is not a crime," the movement declared in a social media poster, using the Hindi name for India's tricolour. It urged supporters to share their photographs online.Opposition parties have also been holding protests against Kumar and the Election Commission.Last week, Rahul Gandhi and other opposition lawmakers were detained while attempting to march to the commission's headquarters. They have also taken their concerns to President Droupadi Murmu and marched towards the Supreme Court.Gandhi has condemned the arrests of CJP leaders and called for Jantar Mantar to be reopened to protesters, although the opposition and the youth-led movement have largely demonstrated separately.Home Minister Amit Shah has accused the opposition of spreading falsehoods about the voter-list revision and defended the commission's independence.For the CJP, the immediate question is how long it can sustain its protests with its three main leaders in custody.Pasricha said the party had a team and a plan in place. "If the top three continue to stay behind bars, we will continue to protest peacefully," she said.

schema.headline: CJP, Abhijeet Dipke: 'Cockroach' party founder detained ahead of Central Park Delhi protest
